name: Quantization and Model Compression
intent: Understand how a model's weights can be stored in fewer bits, or learned by a smaller model, so that it fits on cheaper hardware, and what that costs in accuracy.
scenario: A 70-billion-parameter model needs 140 GB just for its weights in 16-bit numbers. That is more than one 80 GB GPU holds, and the team would like to serve it on as few GPUs as possible.
problem: A model's weights are billions of numbers, and every generated token has to read all of them from memory. In 16-bit format each weight takes two bytes, so a large model needs several GPUs before any request has been served, and the reading of those bytes limits speed. Storing each weight in fewer bits, or using a smaller model that behaves like the large one, cuts both the memory and the traffic, if the loss in accuracy is small enough to accept.

howItWorks.title: Weights are just numbers
howItWorks.text: A model's weights are usually stored as 16-bit floating-point numbers, two bytes each. The memory for the weights is the number of parameters times the bytes per weight: 70 billion x 2 bytes = 140 GB.

howItWorks.title: Quantization rounds to fewer levels
howItWorks.text: To store a weight in 8 bits, pick a scale, divide the weight by it, round to the nearest integer between -127 and 127, and keep the integer and the scale. To use the weight later, multiply back. The result is close to the original, not equal to it.

howItWorks.title: Outliers are the hard part
howItWorks.text: If one weight in a block is much larger than the rest, the scale must stretch to cover it, and all the other weights are squeezed into a few levels. Many methods use a separate scale for each small group of weights for that reason. A related problem is in the activations: the LLM.int8 paper found a few large outlier feature dimensions in the hidden states of big transformers, and multiplied those in 16-bit while more than 99.9 percent of the values were multiplied in 8-bit.

howItWorks.title: Post-training methods go down to 4 bits
howItWorks.text: Post-training quantization converts a finished model without retraining it. LLM.int8 reported halving inference memory while keeping full-precision quality. GPTQ reported compressing 175-billion-parameter models to 3 or 4 bits per weight in about four GPU hours, with little loss in accuracy. Results differ by model and task, so measure on yours.

howItWorks.title: Distillation trains a smaller student
howItWorks.text: Instead of shrinking the numbers, distillation trains a smaller model to imitate a larger one. The student learns from the teacher's output probabilities (soft targets), which carry more information per example than a single correct label. Pruning, which removes weights that matter least, is a third route.

howItWorks.title: Measure, do not assume
howItWorks.text: The memory saving is exact: halve the bits, halve the weights' memory. The accuracy cost is not. Compare the compressed model with the original on perplexity and on your own tasks, including the rare and hard cases. Remember that the KV cache and activations still need memory on top of the weights.

pros: Memory for the weights falls in proportion to the bits: 8-bit halves it, 4-bit quarters it
Fewer bytes to read per token can speed up generation, when the hardware supports the format
A model that fits on fewer GPUs is cheaper to serve
Post-training methods need no retraining of the model
cons: Some accuracy is lost, and how much depends on the model, the method and the task
Outliers and unusual inputs can suffer more than the average case does
Not every format runs fast on every GPU, so the speed-up is not guaranteed
The KV cache and activations are not reduced by quantizing the weights alone
whenToUse: The model does not fit in your GPU memory at full precision
Serving cost is dominated by the number of GPUs the weights need
You can measure quality on your own tasks before and after
whenNotToUse: Do not quantize aggressively without an evaluation set that includes your hard cases
Do not assume the saving applies to the KV cache, which has its own size
Do not use a method or format your serving hardware cannot run efficiently
pitfalls: Judging quality on average benchmarks only, and missing a drop on your own rare cases
Using one scale for a whole matrix, so that a single outlier ruins the precision of the rest
Counting only the weights when sizing GPUs, then running out of memory for the KV cache
Mixing up distillation (a different, smaller model) with quantization (the same model in fewer bits)

roles.label: Full-precision weights
roles.description: The model as trained, usually 16-bit numbers.

roles.label: Quantizer
roles.description: Chooses scales and rounds each weight to a small integer.

roles.label: Compact weights
roles.description: Small integers plus scales: a fraction of the memory.

roles.label: Inference runtime
roles.description: Multiplies the integers by their scales while serving, ideally with hardware support.

quiz.question: A 70-billion-parameter model needs 140 GB for its weights in 16-bit form, and the team's GPUs have 80 GB each. What does converting the weights to 8-bit do?
options: It halves the weights to about 70 GB, which may fit on one GPU, but the KV cache still needs room as well
It removes the need for a KV cache, so only the weights have to fit in memory
It makes no difference to memory, because the model's number of parameters is unchanged
It quarters the weights to 35 GB, because 8-bit numbers are half the size of 16-bit ones
quiz.explanation: Memory for the weights is parameters times bytes each: 70 billion at one byte is about 70 GB, half of 140. That may fit on one 80 GB GPU, but the KV cache and activations need memory as well. Quantizing the weights does not remove the cache, and 4-bit, not 8-bit, would give 35 GB.

quiz.question: When weights are quantized with one scale for a whole block, a single very large weight is present in the block. What is the most likely effect on the other weights?
options: They become more precise, because the larger value pulls the scale towards the average
They are unchanged, since each weight is rounded on its own and the scale does not matter
They are removed from the model and stored in a separate file
They are squeezed into a few levels and lose precision, which is why methods use finer scales or handle outliers separately
quiz.explanation: The scale must cover the largest value, so the steps between levels become coarse for all the smaller ones. Using a separate scale for each small group of weights avoids this. LLM.int8 deals with a different kind of outlier, large feature dimensions in the activations, by multiplying them in 16-bit. The other options describe things quantization does not do.

quiz.question: What is the difference between distilling a model and quantizing it?
options: They are two names for the same technique, used by different research groups
Distillation stores the weights in fewer bits, while quantization removes layers from the model
Distillation trains a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher, while quantization keeps the same model and stores its numbers in fewer bits
Quantization needs the original training data, while distillation never needs any data at all
quiz.explanation: Distillation produces a different, smaller model trained on the teacher's outputs. Quantization converts the same model's numbers to a lower precision. They are different techniques that can be combined. Post-training quantization usually needs only a small sample of data, and distillation does need data to train the student.
